segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In Iconium the same thing happened: they went into the synagogue of the Jews and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and embittered their souls against the brothers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they stayed a considerable time, speaking boldly in reliance on the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace by granting signs and wonders to be done through their hands.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the people of the city were divided: some were with the Jews and some with the apostles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When a move was made by both Gentiles and Jews, together with their leaders, to abuse them and stone them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: they learned of it and fled to the cities of Lycaonia, Lystra and Derbe, and to the surrounding region,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and there they went on proclaiming the good news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In Lystra there sat a man who had no use of his feet, lame from his mother’s womb, who had never walked.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This man listened to Paul speaking. Paul looked straight at him and, seeing that he had faith to be made well,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: said in a loud voice,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Stand up straight on your feet!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he sprang up and began to walk.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voices and said in Lycaonian,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “The gods have become like human beings and come down to us!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, because he was the one who took the lead in speaking.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The priest of Zeus, whose temple stood just outside the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice together with the crowds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their clothes and rushed out into the crowd, shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Men, why are you doing this? We too are human beings, of the same nature as you, bringing you the good news that you should turn from these worthless things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: In past generations he let all the nations go their own ways;

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: yet he did not leave himself without witness: he did good, giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even with these words they barely stopped the crowds from sacrificing to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium and won over the crowds. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, supposing that he was dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But when the disciples gathered around him, he got up and went into the city. The next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After they had proclaimed the good news to that city and made a considerable number of disciples, they returned to Lystra, to Iconium, and to Antioch,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: strengthening the souls of the disciples and urging them to continue in the faith, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is through many hardships that we must enter the kingdom of God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After appointing elders for them in each assembly, with prayer and fasting they entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had come to believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and after speaking the word in Perga they went down to Attalia.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they arrived, they gathered the assembly together and reported all that God had done with them, and that he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they stayed no short time with the disciples.

notes.traditional: they went both together into the synagogue
notes.note: The Greek phrase kata to auto can mean either "in the same way" (as at Pisidian Antioch in the previous chapter) or "together." Older versions and some modern ones take it as "together"; many recent translations take it as "in the same way" or "as usual." The rendering here follows the second reading, which fits the repeated pattern of synagogue preaching, a divided response and expulsion.

A single Greek word, ethnē, lies behind both "Gentiles" (verses 2, 5, 27) and "nations" (verse 16). In Jewish usage the plural meant the non-Jewish peoples. It is rendered "nations" where the peoples of the world as a whole are in view, and "Gentiles" where non-Jews are contrasted with Jews.

Only here and in verse 14 does Acts call Paul and Barnabas "apostles"; elsewhere in the book the term is kept for the Twelve. The word means an authorised envoy. Many scholars think it is used here of the two as emissaries sent out by the assembly at Antioch (13:1-3).

The Greek verb covers both physical rescue or healing and salvation in the fuller religious sense. Here the immediate meaning is healing. Luke often lets the wider sense sound alongside it, and some translators render it "to be saved."

Zeus was the chief of the Greek gods and Hermes was the gods' messenger and spokesman, which is why Paul, the speaker, is identified as Hermes. A legend told by the Roman poet Ovid has Zeus and Hermes visiting this general region in human disguise and being refused hospitality by all but one elderly couple. Such a story may explain the crowd's eagerness not to repeat the mistake.

The Greek does not say which gates are meant. They may be the city gates, the gates of the temple precinct outside the city, or the gateway of the house where Paul and Barnabas were staying. The Greek speaks literally of "the Zeus who is before the city," a way of naming the god by his shrine's location; "whose temple stood" makes that explicit.

In the Greek Old Testament this word ("empty, futile") is a regular term for idols and the gods they represent. The apostles are speaking of the gods the crowd is about to sacrifice to. The description of God that follows, maker of heaven, earth, sea and everything in them, echoes Exodus 20:11 and Psalm 146:6.

The verb originally described voting by a show of hands, and some interpreters argue that the congregations elected their elders. By this period it was widely used simply for "appoint," and the grammar here makes Paul and Barnabas the ones who do it. "Ordained" in older versions imports a later church rite.

The traditional rendering is "church," which is near-universal and which readers understand. A first-century hearer, however, knew this word as the ordinary term for a civic gathering and as the Greek Old Testament's word for Israel assembled, whereas "church" now suggests a building or an institution. "Assembly" is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word; it means the community of believers in a place, not a single meeting.

Two different cities are called Antioch in this chapter. In verses 19 and 21 it is Antioch near Pisidia in central Asia Minor, where Paul preached in chapter 13. Here it is the great city of Antioch in Syria, whose assembly had sent Paul and Barnabas out (13:1-3) and to which they now report back.

candidates.reason: It ranges over life, self, inner person and mind, and translations vary between 'soul', 'mind', 'life' and a bare pronoun; readers will be misled if the English shifts without a rule.
It recurs across the Gospels, Paul and Revelation and is variously rendered 'tribulation', 'affliction', 'persecution', 'suffering' and 'hardship'; one decision by sense is needed.
